samples.summary: Merge-expansion work budget removed from the copy/cut/delete path: a peer-authored table can now freeze the victim's tab on an ordinary Ctrl+C or Delete
samples.evidence: Before this delta `normalizeCellRange` always passed `MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS` into `expandCellRangeForMerges`. It now defaults to `budgetCells = Infinity` (selection.ts:205, used at 223) and only `computeSelectionRects` (selection.ts:717) supplies the bound, so every caller reaching `Selection.getNormalizedRange` (selection.ts:905) runs the expansion unbounded: `getSelectedText` (selection.ts:919, copy/cut), `getSelectedTableCells` (text-editor.ts:4322), `getSelectedBlocks` (text-editor.ts:4363) and the cell-rectangle delete (text-editor.ts:4165). `expandCellRangeForMerges` is a fixed-point `while (changed)` loop that rescans the whole rectangle each pass and, for every covered cell, calls `findMergeTopLeftBudgeted` which scans the entire area above-left (selection.ts:135-161, 90-104). All of its inputs are peer-controlled: rows are CRDT structure with no numeric band (a peer can write 10^5 rows) and `colSpan`/`rowSpan` come off the wire (banded only to MAX_TABLE_SPAN=1000). Attack: a collaborator (or anyone with write access to the shared Yorkie doc) writes a table with a staircase of merges — each pass grows the rectangle by one row, so passes ≈ rows and each pass costs O(rows*cols) — or a field of orphan `colSpan: 0` cells whose owner never existed, each costing an O(r*c) backtrack. The victim only has to drag-select cells in that table and press Ctrl+C or Delete; the main thread then spins for minutes-to-forever. This is the same 'one peer's data hangs everyone's tab' hazard the file's own MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS comment describes, re-opened for the act paths. A bound that clamps the rectangle after expansion (or a budget that is large but finite on the act paths too) would keep the 'exactness' argument for realistic tables while still degrading instead of hanging on hostile ones.

samples.summary: The new truncated-rows refusal is gated on the *new* model content, so a replacing write whose replacement no longer carries the table-at-the-cap skips the tree check and still deletes rows it never read
samples.evidence: `updateBlock` only consults the CRDT (`assertReplacesNoTruncatedRows`, line 1834) when `hasTableAtNestingCap([block], blockDepth)` is true for the block being written (line 1833); `updateTableCell` does the same on `cell.blocks` (line 3021). The destructive condition, however, lives in the *old* tree content at that path, not in the replacement. Any replacing write whose new model no longer contains a table at MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH bypasses the tree check entirely and overwrites the node — deleting a peer's rows and replicating that deletion — which is exactly the outcome `treeHasTruncatedRows` was added to prevent. Reachable examples of a replacement that drops the truncated table from the model: `Doc.mergeCells` writes emptied covered cells through `store.updateTableCell` (packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:1184), and the cell-rectangle delete replaces every selected cell's blocks with a fresh empty paragraph and then calls `updateBlockDirect` on the whole table block (packages/docs/src/view/text-editor.ts:4177-4185). Both cases can be argued as user-intended deletes, which is why confidence is low, but the user never saw the rows being destroyed and the guard's own docstring claims the check is made 'against the rows the CRDT actually holds under the range they are about to overwrite' — which is only true when the replacement happens to still contain a capped table. Checking the tree unconditionally for the replaced path (or at least whenever the old model had a capped table under it) would close the gap.

samples.summary: `assertReplacesNoTruncatedRows` fails open (or throws TypeError) when the tree path does not resolve
samples.evidence: `getTreeBlockNode` (line 1231) walks `((node as ElementNode).children ?? [])[idx]` with no bounds check. If any intermediate index is out of range the next iteration dereferences `undefined.children` and the guard throws a bare `TypeError` instead of its intended refusal; if only the final index is out of range it returns `undefined` and `treeHasTruncatedRows(undefined, depth)` returns `false` (line 486), so the destructive replacement proceeds unchecked. The paths come from `resolveBlockTreePath` over the *cached* model, and this same file documents that the cache and the tree can disagree about a block's children ('Read inline count from the actual tree, not the cache, because previous split/merge operations can leave the tree with a different number of inline nodes than the cache', line 2795). A safety check that silently answers 'safe' when it cannot resolve the node is the wrong default for a guard whose failure mode is replicated data deletion; it should fail closed (refuse) when the node cannot be resolved.

samples.summary: A peer can plant rows past the nesting cap and make ordinary local table edits throw an uncaught exception, denying those edits to every other user
samples.evidence: The delta moves the refusal from the whole-document writer onto interactive incremental writers (`updateBlock` line 1834, `updateTableCell` line 3022, `setHeader` line 1016, `setFooter` line 1062). The precondition — a table node at/past MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH that still has row children — is entirely peer-authored: the local UI refuses to create it (`Doc.insertTable`, packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:925) but a scripted peer can write it with raw Yorkie tree edits, and the PR's own test builds exactly that shape (`peerRowsPastTheCap`, packages/frontend/tests/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.test.ts). Once planted, every replacing write over the enclosing block (table structural edits, cell paste, cell-rectangle delete, merges) throws for every collaborator, permanently and across reloads, and there is no error boundary in packages/frontend (no `ErrorBoundary`/`componentDidCatch` anywhere under packages/frontend/src), so the refusal surfaces as an uncaught exception from a DOM event handler rather than as a handled, explained refusal. The batch wrapper (`Doc.batch`, packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:198) does re-read the model so the local cache is not left diverged, which limits this to a lost edit plus an uncaught error — but the denial is peer-triggerable and permanent for that region of the document. Worth catching at the editor boundary and surfacing a message instead of letting it escape.

verdict.reason: Every element of the claim checks out in the tree. `normalizeCellRange` (selection.ts:202-206) and `normalizeRange` (selection.ts:262-266) both default `budgetCells = Infinity` and forward it to `expandCellRangeForMerges` (selection.ts:222-224, 282-286); `computeSelectionRects` (selection.ts:715) is the sole caller passing `MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS` (selection.ts:53), a fact the file's own comment states outright (selection.ts:25-36). `Selection.getNormalizedRange` (selection.ts:905) therefore runs the expansion unbounded for the act paths: copy/cut via `getSelectedText` (selection.ts:918-946), the cell-rectangle delete (text-editor.ts:4165-4185), `getSelectedTableCells` (text-editor.ts:4322) and `getSelectedBlocks` (text-editor.ts:4363). The expansion is a fixed-point `while (changed)` loop rescanning the rectangle each pass (selection.ts:135-161) with an O(r*c) above-left backtrack per `colSpan === 0` cell (selection.ts:90-104); with `budget.left = Infinity` neither early-exit fires. Inputs are peer-controlled: spans are banded only to MAX_TABLE_SPAN = 1000 (numeric-attrs.ts:92, 218) and a repo-wide grep found no band on table row count, matching the file's own note (selection.ts:38-41). No upstream guard bounds it — the clamp at selection.ts:207-219 bounds the rectangle to the table, not the table's size, and the layout clamp at selection.ts:821-824 is on the paint path only and downstream of the expansion. A hostile table from any doc collaborator freezes the victim's main thread on an ordinary Ctrl+C or Delete; this is untrusted-input-driven resource exhaustion, the same hazard class the codebase bands elsewhere, so it is in the security lane and I have no named ground to refute it.

verdict.reason: The described gap is real in code — `updateBlock` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:1833-1835) and `updateTableCell` (3021-3026) gate the CRDT check `assertReplacesNoTruncatedRows` (1748-1752) on `hasTableAtNestingCap` of the *replacement* model, so a replacement that no longer contains a table at MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH skips the tree check before the whole-node `editByPath` (1847, 3033-3037). But it is out of scope for the Security lens: the guard is a data-integrity protection against this reader's own read-time truncation (`treeNodeToBlock` reporting capped tables as `rows: []`), not a permission gate. No trust boundary is crossed — the only access-control state here is `readOnly` (839-843, enforced at 1553/3662/3692) and it is untouched, and every actor in the described scenario (the writer, the peer, `Doc.mergeCells` at packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:1184, the rectangle delete at packages/docs/src/view/text-editor.ts:4185) is an already-authorized editor who could delete those rows through ordinary table edits, so there is no escalation, IDOR, or cross-document reach. It is also not secrets, injection (paths are integer index arrays passed to Yorkie `editByPath`), path traversal, SSRF, deserialization, or a crypto/signature check. The residual harm — silent loss of a peer's rows under a 32-deep nested table, plus a docstring that overclaims coverage — is a general logic/data-loss bug belonging to the correctness lens, which this rubric explicitly tells me to defer.
